Vietnamese Tourism Sites Hit by Severe Flooding, Firms Face Ongoing Disruption

Vietnam’s tourism industry is grappling with widespread disruption as severe flooding continues to inundate key destinations in the country’s central region. Persistent torrential rains over the past week have caused rivers to overflow, damaging several major tourist sites and forcing temporary closures at resorts, cultural attractions, and ecotourism facilities.

At present, floodwaters have inundated large sections of the historic Hoi An Ancient Town and the riverside areas of Hue, two of Vietnam’s most visited heritage sites. The popular Sun Lotus Eco-Resort, located on the outskirts of Hoi An, reported extensive water damage to its guest villas and recreational areas. “All of our ground-floor facilities are under water, and we have had to relocate both guests and staff to higher ground,” said Tran Van Hoang, spokesperson for Sun Lotus Eco-Resort. “Safety is our top priority, and we are working closely with local authorities.”

Firms operating river tours and cultural excursions have also been forced to suspend operations. According to the Vietnam Association of Tourism Operators, over 60 percent of tour companies in the affected areas have halted their activities for the time being, with many expressing concern over the prospects for the peak summer travel season.

“Every day the flooding continues, the losses mount,” said Nguyen Thi Linh, chairwoman of the Central Vietnam Tourism Union. “Many of our member firms are facing significant financial strain, and some have reported that they may not be able to pay full wages to their workers this month.”

Local tourism workers are bearing the brunt of the disruption. In Hoi An, nearly 1,500 guides, hospitality staff, and maintenance workers have been temporarily sent home or reassigned to emergency duties such as sandbagging and protecting assets from water damage. “We are doing our best to keep our teams safe and provide them with support, but the situation is very challenging,” said Duong Minh Quang, director of the Lantern Heritage Tours company.

The floods are also affecting tourism farms and adventure parks in the region, with several reporting damage to hiking trails, equipment, and guest lodges. Industry analysts estimate that losses to the tourism sector could reach 160 billion VND if the flooding persists through the end of the month.

With weather forecasts predicting continued heavy rainfall, tourism firms are bracing for further impacts. The Vietnam Association of Tourism Operators has called for urgent support measures to help affected businesses and workers navigate the crisis.
